title: Back quickly
hook: when events shake you, return to yourself quickly (Meditations 6.11)
carry: give the peg a quick twist

segments.voice: Yesterday: the best revenge, not becoming like the one who wronged you. Your line was not like them.

A guitarist is halfway through a song when a string slips flat. Everyone hears it. A beginner keeps playing out of tune to the end, mortified. A seasoned player gives the peg a quick twist between phrases and is back in tune before the chorus. Nobody remembers the sour note. They remember the song. Marcus Aurelius uses almost exactly that picture for a shaken mind. The question isn't whether you'll be knocked out of tune. It's how long you stay there.
screen: `A STRING SLIPS FLAT.` → `A QUICK TWIST OF THE PEG.` → `HOW LONG YOU STAY OUT OF TUNE.`

segments.voice: Meditations six, eleven, starts by admitting that circumstances will sometimes force you to be disturbed. Marcus doesn't pretend a Stoic floats above every shock. Then, in George Long's translation, he tells himself to "quickly return to thyself, and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts." The word quickly matters. Not never wobble: come back fast. The shock is real for as long as it's happening. Staying shaken after it's over is the optional part. The word he uses is harmony, the Greek harmonia, a word for musical tuning and fitting together. You'll have more mastery over the harmony, he says, by continually returning to it. Mastery doesn't come from never slipping. It comes from coming back so often that the way back gets short. A musician who has retuned over and over can do it without stopping the song. Modern people have their own words for this. Psychologists talk about recovery time after stress, and some meditation teachers say the moment you notice you've drifted is the moment of practice, not of failure. Those are separate traditions with their own reasons, and none of them is quoting Marcus. But they share his picture. A week ago, in 5.9, Marcus came back after failing. Here the point is speed: how soon you come back after being shaken.
screen: `SHOCKS WILL SHAKE YOU.` · `RETURN TO YOURSELF QUICKLY.` · `MASTERY BY RETURNING OFTEN.` · `THE REP IS COMING BACK.` · then, large: `BACK QUICKLY.`

segments.voice: Follow your breath in and out. Before long a thought or a sound will pull you off, and that's just the string slipping. When you notice, give the peg a little twist and come back to the next breath, without scolding; each return is the whole practice.
Back quickly. Marcus's instruction for a shaken mind: you'll be knocked out of tune, so come back fast and often. Today's word.
Your line: give the peg a quick twist. The shock is real; staying shaken is optional. Five hundred seventy-five, and counting.

howItsDone: Some people who practice meditation or Stoic reflection treat each return from distraction or upset as the exercise itself, aiming to shorten the time they stay shaken rather than to never be shaken.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Stoic should never get rattled.
what it means: you'll be rattled; come back fast, and keep coming back until the way back is short.
what a scholar hears: harmonia first meant a joint or fitting in carpentry and shipbuilding, then a musical tuning; Marcus uses the musical sense.
